title: Killer Whales Are Literally Exploding Sunfish — Here's Why
summary:
Orcas are famous for wild hunting moves: punting seals into the air, slapping stingrays, knocking penguins off ice. Now add one more to the list — using a dead sunfish as a piñata.

In 2024 and 2025, scientists documented this behavior in the Gulf of California. In each case, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady while a second orca slammed into it with enough force to smash it to smithereens. The findings appeared July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.

Why do it? One leading idea is food prep. Sharp-tail sunfish can reach a few meters (about 10 feet) long — a huge meal. Breaking one into smaller pieces could help feed young orcas. After one explosion, a juvenile orca fed on the bits.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who wasn't part of the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

But feeding may not be the whole story. "Killer whales are highly social animals," noted Francesca Pancaldi, a marine biologist at Mexico's National Polytechnic Institute. A single activity, she explained, can provide nutrition, strengthen bonds, and teach young orcas how to hunt — all at once.

Nyegaard isn't surprised orcas invented this trick. "They are so clever at figuring out how to hunt and deal with a ton of different prey types," she said. Orcas already work as a team to ambush blue whales and whale sharks. Smashing a sunfish is just one more example of their creativity — and their appetite.
why_it_matters: Orca behavior matters beyond one dramatic sighting: it shows how much of the ocean's top predators' culture humans still have not seen, and it has practical weight for conservation, because if orcas depend on prey such as sunfish and whale sharks, changes in those populations ripple upward through the food web. It is also a reminder that much of what we know about animal intelligence comes from rare, opportunistic observations rather than planned experiments.

background_read: Orcas (also called killer whales, and actually the largest species in the dolphin family) live in every ocean and hunt in tight family groups.
Different populations specialize in different prey — some eat fish, others ambush seals, dolphins and even whales — which is why scientists call them some of the most versatile predators on Earth.

The Gulf of California (the narrow sea between Mexico's Baja California peninsula and the mainland, sometimes nicknamed the 'aquarium of the world') is one of the richest marine ecosystems on the planet, so it is a natural place to spot unusual hunting behavior.

Auckland Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira, in New Zealand) is where Marianne Nyegaard works; she is the marine biologist who first described the hoodwinker sunfish, a species that had hidden in plain sight for centuries.

Ocean sunfish are the heaviest bony fish in the world, and a sharp-tail sunfish is a close relative — so a meal that size is worth smashing apart. Frontiers in Ethology, where the findings appeared, is a journal devoted to ethology, the study of animal behavior.

perspectives.description: For behavioral scientists, this is fresh evidence of how inventive and flexible orcas are, and because a juvenile fed on the broken pieces, it hints at social learning — young orcas may pick up techniques by watching adults. It also shows that patient observation from boats can still reveal completely new behavior.

Only a couple of cases were documented, which is a very small sample; researchers cannot yet say this is a regular habit or that the food-prep explanation is correct. Watching and following wild orcas closely can also disturb them, so there is a cost to collecting this kind of footage.

Orcas are famous for population-specific traditions: different groups have their own diets, calls and hunting methods that are passed down socially rather than built in. Seen that way, smashing a sunfish looks less like a freak event and more like another example of animal culture in action.

More sightings — including reports and footage from fishers and tourists — could show how often this happens and whether the trick spreads between orcas. As oceans warm and prey shift, the ability to improvise new hunting methods may help decide which orca populations thrive and which struggle.
